title: Medical-isotopes chain

chokepoint.physics: Mo-99 is made in a handful of ageing research reactors; a 66-hour half-life means no stockpile is possible — an irreplaceable, buffer-less capability

eyebrow: Product-chain pilot · the scan you might need
h1: The world's most-used medical isotope is made in about six ageing reactors — and can't be stored
deck: Technetium-99m images tens of millions of patients a year — bones, hearts, tumours. It is milked from molybdenum-99, which is produced in only a handful of ageing research reactors. And because Mo-99 decays with a 66-hour half-life, none of it can be stockpiled: when one reactor goes down for maintenance, hospitals worldwide run short within days.
byline: research reactor (few, ageing) ≠ Mo-99 (66h half-life, no stockpile) ≠ Tc-99m generator ≠ the scan
correction: This chain is a chokepoint of a different kind — not concentration for leverage, but fragility. The isotope behind ~40 million diagnostic scans a year, technetium-99m, comes from molybdenum-99 made in roughly six research reactors (in the Netherlands, Belgium, and a few others), most of them decades old. Mo-99's short half-life makes stockpiling impossible, so a single reactor outage cascades into global shortages. The risk is an irreplaceable, buffer-less capability, not a hostile supplier.

sections.h2: 1 · A supply chain that races the clock

panels.text: Molybdenum-99 loses about 1% of its activity per hour, so from the moment it leaves the reactor it is decaying. There is no way to build a strategic reserve — the entire chain, from irradiation to the patient, runs in days. That is what makes a routine reactor shutdown a clinical emergency: you cannot draw down a stock that physically cannot exist.

The bulk of world Mo-99 has come from a small set of research reactors built in the 1960s-70s — the Netherlands' HFR at Petten, Belgium's BR2, and a few others — with periodic gaps as they age and undergo refurbishment. Canada's NRU, once a mainstay, closed in 2018. Each retirement thins an already thin supply, which is why the sector lives with recurring shortage scares.

Technetium-99m is used in roughly 80% of nuclear-medicine procedures — bone scans, cardiac perfusion, kidney function, sentinel-node cancer staging — because it emits a clean imaging gamma and clears the body quickly. There is no drop-in substitute for many of these scans, so a Mo-99 shortage directly delays cancer staging and cardiac diagnosis for patients.

sections.h2: 3 · The fix: spread and modernise production

panels.h3: New routes, no more weapons uranium
panels.text: The response is to diversify and modernise: converting production off highly-enriched (weapons-grade) uranium targets to low-enriched ones, adding new reactor and accelerator-based routes, and building capacity in more countries. It is a capability-rebuilding problem — funding and qualifying new production over years — the same shape as enrichment or turbine blades, but for a material that images the sick.

trade_intro: BACI carries radioactive isotopes and compounds in one broad line (284440); Mo-99 and Tc-99m cannot be isolated, and because they decay in hours much of the real flow is time-critical air freight that customs statistics capture poorly. Read the shares below as the broad radioisotope basket only, not a medical-isotope series.
